manuscript_meta.title: ENERGY-BASED GENERATIVE ADVERSARIAL NET- WORKS Junbo Zhao, Michael Mathieu and Yann LeCun Department of Computer Science, New York University

report.summary: This paper introduces Energy-based Generative Adversarial Networks (EBGANs), a novel framework that recasts the GAN discriminator as an energy function rather than a probabilistic classifier. The core idea is to train the discriminator to assign low energy to data points on the real data manifold and high energy elsewhere. The generator, in turn, learns to produce samples with minimal energy. The authors instantiate this framework by using an auto-encoder as the discriminator, where the reconstruction error serves as the energy. The paper provides theoretical justification for this approach, proving that the generator's distribution converges to the data distribution at equilibrium. Empirically, it demonstrates through extensive experiments on MNIST, LSUN, CelebA, and ImageNet that EBGANs exhibit greater training stability than traditional GANs and can generate high-resolution (up to 256x256) images without requiring a multi-scale architecture.

points: The reframing of GANs within an energy-based modeling framework is a significant conceptual leap. It generalizes the GAN objective and provides greater flexibility in the choice of discriminator architecture and loss functions, moving beyond the standard binary classifier.

The specific instantiation of the discriminator as an auto-encoder is elegant and well-motivated. It connects two major families of unsupervised learning models (GANs and auto-encoders) in a principled way.

The work addresses a critical and widely-recognized problem in GAN research: training instability. The proposed method offers a practical solution that is shown to be more robust across a wide range of hyperparameters.

The paper provides a formal proof (Theorem 1 & 2) that, under a hinge loss, the EBGAN framework has a Nash equilibrium where the generator distribution matches the data distribution. This adds significant theoretical rigor to the proposed model.
The empirical evaluation is comprehensive and convincing. The large-scale grid search on MNIST provides strong quantitative evidence for the claim of improved stability compared to standard GANs.

The qualitative results are impressive, particularly the generation of 128x128 and 256x256 images on the complex ImageNet dataset using a single-scale generator. This was a notable achievement at the time of writing and strongly supports the paper's claims about the model's scalability.

The reference list is in a poor state. As confirmed by the evidence pack, a vast majority of the citations (20 out of 22) could not be automatically resolved against major academic indices. This indicates that the bibliographic entries are likely incomplete or malformed (e.g., missing DOIs, incorrect venue/year, inconsistent author names). This is a critical issue for a scholarly work that must be corrected before publication.

The margin 'm' is presented as a crucial hyperparameter. While Appendix E provides helpful practical tips, the main body of the paper would benefit from a more direct discussion of the model's sensitivity to this parameter. Its tuning appears non-trivial, which could be a practical limitation of the method.

detailed_comments.comment: The most urgent issue to address is the quality of the bibliography. The evidence pack indicates that 20 out of 22 references could not be resolved, including foundational papers like Goodfellow et al. (2014) and Radford et al. (2015). This requires a meticulous review and correction of every entry to include full, accurate, and resolvable information (e.g., DOIs for journal articles, stable arXiv links for preprints, full conference proceedings details).

The description of the semi-supervised learning training procedure (Section 4.2) is split between the main text and Appendix D. For improved clarity, the authors should consider integrating the rationale for key decisions, such as turning off the generator training after 60,000 steps, more directly into the main text.

questions: The margin 'm' is clearly a critical hyperparameter. Beyond the helpful tips in the appendix, have you investigated its effect on mode collapse vs. sample quality? A more quantitative analysis (e.g., using the inception score vs. 'm') would be very insightful.

The Pulling-away Term (PT) is introduced to improve sample diversity. How does this method compare, in terms of both performance and computational overhead, to the 'minibatch discrimination' technique from Salimans et al. (2016), which you cite as having a similar philosophy? A brief discussion would help contextualize this contribution.

Could you please undertake a thorough revision of the reference list to ensure every entry is complete and correct, providing DOIs or other persistent identifiers where available, to fix the resolution issues identified in the evidence pack?
report.overall_assessment: This is an excellent paper presenting a significant and influential contribution to the field of generative models. The core idea of an Energy-Based GAN is novel, theoretically sound, and empirically powerful. The authors convincingly demonstrate that their approach leads to more stable training and is capable of producing high-resolution images, addressing key challenges in the field. The scientific contribution is exceptionally strong. The manuscript is accepted for publication based on its scientific merit. This acceptance is conditional upon a mandatory and thorough revision of the bibliography. As noted by all reviewers and confirmed by the evidence pack, the reference list is in a poor state and requires meticulous correction before the final version can be published. Addressing the minor points of clarification raised in the questions would also strengthen the final manuscript.

In the ﬁrst interpretation, the key component is the generator, and the discriminator plays the role of a trainable objective function. Let us imagine that the data lies on a manifold. Until the generator produces samples that are recognized as being on the manifold, it gets a gradient indicating how to modify its output so it could approach the manifold. In such scenario, the discriminator acts to punish the generator when it produces samples that are outside the manifold. For the second interpretation, the key component is the discriminator, and the generator is merely trained to produce contrastive samples. C APPENDIX: EXPERIMENT SETTINGS MORE DETAILS ABOUT THE GRID SEARCH For training both EBGANs and GANs for the grid search, we use the following setting: • Batch normalization (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015) is applied after each weight layer, except for the generator output layer and the discriminator input layer (Radford et al., 2015). • Training images are scaled into range [-1,1]. Correspondingly the generator output layer is fol- lowed by a Tanh function. • ReLU is used as the non-linearity function. • Initialization: the weights in D from N(0, 0.002) and in G from N(0, 0.02). Speciﬁcally, we utilize an identical architecture as reported in both papers (Rasmus et al., 2015; Pezeshki et al., 2015); namely a fully-connected network of size 784-1000-500-250-250-250, with batch normalization and ReLU following each linear layer. To obtain a strong baseline, we tuned the weight of the reconstruction cost with values from the set { 5000 784 , 2000 784 , 1000 784 , 500 784}, while ﬁxing the weight on the classiﬁcation cost to 1. In the meantime, we also tuned the learning rate with values {0.002, 0.001, 0.0005, 0.0002, 0.0001}. We adopted Adam as the optimizer with β1 being set to 0.5. The minibatch size was set to 100. All the experiments are ﬁnished by 120,000 steps. We use the same learning rate decay mechanism as in the published papers – starting from the two-thirds of total steps (i.e., from step #80,000) to linearly decay the learning rate to 0. The result reported in section 4.2 was done by the best tuned setting: λL2 = 1000 784 , lr = 0.0002. EBGAN-LN MODEL We place the same Ladder Network architecture into our EBGAN framework and train this EBGAN- LN model the same way as we train the EBGAN auto-encoder model. For technical details, we started training the EBGAN-LN model from the margin value 16 and gradually decay it to 0 within the ﬁrst 60,000 steps. By the time, we found that the reconstruction error of the real image had already been low and reached the limitation of the architecture (Ladder Network itself); besides the generated images exhibit good quality (shown in ﬁgure 10). Thereafter we turned off training the generator but kept training the discriminator for another 120,000 steps. We set the initial learning rates to be 0.0005 for discriminator and 0.00025 for generator. The other setting is kept consistent with the best baseline LN model. The learning rate decay started at step #120,000 (also two-thirds of the total steps). 13 OTHER DETAILS • Notice that we used the 28×28 version (unpadded) of the MNIST dataset in the EBGAN-LN experiment. For the EBGAN auto-encoder grid search experiments, we used the zero-padded version, i.e., size 32×32. No phenomenal difference has been found due to the zero-padding. • We generally took the ℓ2 norm of the discrepancy between input and reconstruction for the loss term in the EBGAN auto-encoder model as formally written in section 2.1. However, for the EBGAN-LN experiment, we followed the original implementation of Ladder Network using a vanilla form of ℓ2 loss. • Borrowed from Salimans et al. (2016), the batch normalization is adopted without the learned parameter γ but merely with a bias term β. It still remains unknown whether such trick could affect learning in some non-ignorable way, so this might have made our baseline model not a strict reproduction of the published models by Rasmus et al. (2015) and Pezeshki et al. (2015). E APPENDIX: TIPS FOR SETTING A GOOD ENERGY MARGIN VALUE It is crucial to set a proper energy margin value m in the framework of EBGAN, from both theoretical and experimental perspective. Hereby we provide a few tips: • Delving into the formulation of the discriminator loss made by equation 1, we suggest a numerical balance between its two terms which concern real and fake sample respectively. The second term is apparently bounded by [0, m] (assuming the energy function D(x) is non-negative). It is desirable to make the ﬁrst term bounded in a similar range. In theory, the upper bound of the ﬁrst term is essentially determined by (i)-the capacity of D; (ii)-the complexity of the dataset. • In practice, for the EBGAN auto-encoder model, one can run D (the auto-encoder) alone on the real sample dataset and monitor the loss. When it converges, the consequential loss implies a rough limit on how well such setting of D is capable to ﬁt the dataset. This usually suggests a good start for a hyper-parameter searching on m. • m being overly large results in a training instability/difﬁculty, while m being too small is prone to the mode-dropping problem. This property of m is depicted in ﬁgure 9. • One successful technique, as we introduced in appendix D, is to start from a large m and gradually decayed it to 0 along training proceeds. Unlike the feature matching semi- supervised learning technique proposed by Salimans et al. (2016), we show in ﬁgure 10 that not only does the EBGAN-LN model achieve a good semi-supervised learning perfor- mance, it also produces satisfactory generations. Abstracting away from the practical experimental tips, the theoretical understanding of EBGAN in section 2.2 also provides some insight for setting a feasible m. For instance, as implied by Theorem 2, setting a large m results in a broader range of γ to which D∗(x) may converge. Instability may come after an overly large γ because it generates two strong gradients pointing to opposite directions, from loss 1, which would demand more ﬁnicky optimization setting. F APPENDIX: MORE GENERATION LSUN AUGMENTED VERSION TRAINING For LSUN bedroom dataset, aside from the experiment on the whole images, we also train an EBGAN auto-encoder model based on dataset augmentation by cropping patches. All the patches are of size 64 × 64 and cropped from 96 × 96 original images. The generation is shown in ﬁgure 11. This paper introduces Energy-based Generative Adversarial Networks (EBGANs), a novel framework that recasts the GAN discriminator as an energy function rather than a probabilistic classifier. The core idea is to train the discriminator to assign low energy to data points on the real data manifold and high energy elsewhere. The generator, in turn, learns to produce samples with minimal energy. The authors instantiate this framework by using an auto-encoder as the discriminator, where the reconstruction error serves as the energy. The paper provides theoretical justification for this approach, proving that the generator's distribution converges to the data distribution at equilibrium. Empirically, it demonstrates through extensive experiments on MNIST, LSUN, CelebA, and ImageNet that EBGANs exhibit greater training stability than traditional GANs and can generate high-resolution (up to 256x256) images without requiring a multi-scale architecture.

findings.title: Makale Türüne Özgü Raporlama Kılavuzu Uygulanabilir Değil
findings.summary: Makale, deneysel bir çalışma veya sistematik bir derleme olmadığı için CONSORT, PRISMA, STROBE veya COREQ gibi belirli raporlama kılavuzlarına doğrudan tabi değildir. Bu tür kılavuzlar genellikle klinik deneyler, gözlemsel çalışmalar veya nitel araştırmalar için tasarlanmıştır. Makale, yeni bir makine öğrenimi modeli (EBGAN) sunan ve deneysel sonuçlarını gösteren bir araştırma makalesidir. Bu nedenle, belirli bir raporlama kılavuzuna uyum beklentisi bu bağlamda geçerli değildir.
findings.reasoning_public: Makine öğrenimi alanındaki araştırma makaleleri için genel kabul görmüş, standartlaştırılmış bir raporlama kılavuzu bulunmamaktadır. Bu tür makaleler genellikle metodoloji, deneysel kurulum, sonuçlar ve tartışma gibi standart akademik makale yapısını takip eder. Mevcut makale bu genel yapıya uygun olup, sunulan modelin detaylarını ve deneysel doğrulamalarını içermektedir.

manuscript_anchors.quote: We introduce the “Energy-based Generative Adversarial Network” model (EBGAN) which views the discriminator as an energy function that attributes low energies to the regions near the data manifold and higher energies to other regions.
The essence of the energy-based model (LeCun et al., 2006) is to build a function that maps each point of an input space to a single scalar, which is called “energy”.

Our work primarily casts GANs into an energy-based model scope. On this direction, the approaches studying contrastive samples are relevant to EBGAN, such as the use of noisy samples (Vincent et al., 2010) and noisy gradient descent methods like contrastive divergence (Carreira-Perpinan & Hinton, 2005).

findings.title: Konferans Kapsamına Uygunluk
findings.summary: Makale, derin öğrenme ve üretken modeller alanındaki güncel araştırmaları ele alarak, NIPS gibi önde gelen bir yapay zeka konferansının kapsamına ve teknik düzeyine tamamen uygundur.

manuscript_anchors.quote: We introduce the “Energy-based Generative Adversarial Network” model (EBGAN) which views the discriminator as an energy function that attributes low energies to the regions near the data manifold and higher energies to other regions.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) (Goodfellow et al., 2014) have led to signiﬁcant improve- ments in image generation (Denton et al., 2015; Radford et al., 2015; Im et al., 2016; Salimans et al., 2016), video prediction (Mathieu et al., 2015) and a number of other domains.

We bridge two classes of unsupervised learning methods – GANs and auto-encoders – and revisit the GAN framework from an alternative energy-based perspective. EBGANs show better convergence pattern and scalability to generate high-resolution images.

findings.reasoning_public: Makale, enerji tabanlı modeller ve üretken çekişmeli ağlar (GAN'lar) arasındaki bağlantıyı kurarak, bu iki önemli alanı birleştiren yenilikçi bir yaklaşım sunmaktadır. Sunulan EBGAN modeli, GAN'ların eğitim istikrarı ve yüksek çözünürlüklü görüntü üretimi gibi zorluklarına çözüm getirmeyi amaçlamaktadır. Deneysel sonuçlar, MNIST, LSUN, CelebA ve ImageNet gibi standart veri kümeleri üzerinde modelin performansını göstermektedir. Bu konular ve kullanılan yöntemler (derin öğrenme, sinir ağları, optimizasyon) NIPS gibi konferansların tipik ilgi alanlarına girmektedir.
